§ 298. Liability to gas and electric companies. Except in the case of serious illness, "a gas or electric company may stop gas or electricity from entering the premises of any person failing to pay the amount due therefor or for the use of the meter or other article hired by him from such company; and, for such purpose, the officers, servants or workmen thereof may, after thirty-six hours' notice, enter his premises between the hours of eight in the forenoon and four in the afternoon and separate and take away such meter or other property of the company, and may disconnect any meter, pipe, wires, fittings or other works, whether they are property of the company or not, from its mains, pipes, or wires." 1 "A gas or electric company shall not refuse to supply gas or electricity for any building or premises to a person applying therefor who is not in arrears to it for any gas or electricity previously supplied to him, because a bill for gas or electricity remains unpaid by a previous occupant of such building or premises." 2

Thus the company cannot refuse to supply gas to a voluntary assignee of a corporation because of an unpaid bill of the corporation.3

For a violation of this section the plaintiff has a remedy at law by mandamus, and cannot go into equity for a mandatory injunction, the failure to supply gas being a negative act.* 

Payment may be required in advance or a deposit demanded."

Contributory negligence of tenant. It is stated in an early case that the landlord cannot recover damages from a third person for an injury occasioned partly by such third person and partly by the contributory negligence of his tenant. This conclusion does not rest upon the ground of any personal relation of agency between the landlord and his tenant, but upon the relation of the latter to the property as having the present control and charge of it, and therefore the one was liable to the landlord both in trespass de bonis asportatis and trespass quare clausum fregit.

CHAPTER VIII  

§ 306. In General. The original Bankruptcy Act which took effect in 1898 contained no special provisions as to landlord and tenant. The law was administered until 1934 on the basis that, except for past due rent which of course was an ordinary provable claim, the bankrupt remained liable on the lease. It followed that claims for damages for future rent, however measured, or similar claims for breaches of other covenants in the lease, if maturing after the bankruptcy by entry or otherwise were not provable. The only exception, which lasted only a few months until the amendment hereinafter referred to, was a claim for damages arising from a breach of the so-called ipso facto covenant; that is, a covenant that the filing of a petition in itself terminated the lease without the necessity of any action by the landlord or the trustee.

As this situation led to great confusion and inequity, the first major amendment in this respect to the Bankruptcy Act was passed in 1934. It provided that claims for future rents were provable, but that the claim of a landlord for such rents or damages under the covenants of the lease should not be allowed in an amount exceeding one year's rent from the date of surrender of the premises or the date of re-entry whichever first occurred, plus unpaid rent accrued to that date. Similar, although not identical, provisions were added by the Act of June 22, 1938, and are now found in Chapter X (Corporate Reorganizations), Chapter XI (Arrangements), Chapter XII (Real Estate Arrangements) and Chapter XIII (Wage Earners' Plans). It is important to note, however, that in Chapter XIII the claims are

In the absence of a specific clause that terminates the lease automatically, or allows the landlord to enter and terminate, the trustee may either assume or reject the lease within the time limited. If he assumes it he may later assign it in spite of a general covenant against assignment.¹ If he assumes it, he is, of course, chargeable on the covenants of the lease (except against assignment) like any other assignee and must pay the stipulated rent during his term. He is so liable, however, only through privity of estate and not of contract.2 

If he rejects such a lease, however, there is an automatic provable claim for damages (limited as noted in § 321) from the date of bankruptcy and neither he, nor the lessee, are liable further on the covenants of the lease. Such rejection is a breach and in effect terminates the lease except for the claim to damages. 

With termination clause. If there is an automatic termination clause, or if the landlord can by the terms of the lease enter and terminate and if he does so, the trustee cannot assume the lease, but the landlord is limited to his claim for damages.*

§ § 308. Effect on lease itself (bankruptcy of assignee or sublessee). There appears to be considerable doubt whether a termination clause in a lease applying by its terms only to the lessee will run with the land and bind the assignee.¹ Certainly the general doctrine against granting a forfeiture makes the Court slow to give the landlord the benefit of such a clause in the bankruptcy of an assignee or sub-lessee. For example, forfeiture was denied where the lease referred to the lessee, or of any successor,² and where it referred only to the lessee in spite of a general clause stating that the covenants of the lease were binding on the parties and their assigns. If the lease specifically refers to the lessee "or other tenant" (or assignee), it has been held otherwise. To be on the safe side (1) the lease should specifically refer to bankruptcy of the assignee or sub-lessee and, (2) the assignee should specifically agree with the landlord to be bound by the covenants of the lease on the landlord's consent to the assignment. 3 § 309. Termination clause-Form. Such a clause may be either in a form that automatically terminates the lease (so-called ipso facto clause), or a form that gives the landlord an option to terminate, and is probably better for present day purposes.

The first part of the covenant may be the same in either case. "Provided also that this lease is upon this condition that if the lessee (which expression shall specifically include in this paragraph as well as others where the context so admits, any assignee or sub-lessee) shall neglect or fail to perform or observe any of the lessee's covenants, or if the leasehold hereby created shall be taken on execution, or by other process of law, or if any assignment be made of the lessee's property for the benefit of creditors, or if a receiver, guardian, conservator, trustee in bankruptcy or similar officer shall be appointed to take charge of all or any part of the lessee's property, or if the lessee commits any act of bankruptcy, or if a petition filed by or against the lessee under any bankruptcy law¹ (and in the latter case not dismissed within thirty days after filing) then, and in any of these cases:-" § 308. 1 In re Clerc Chemical Corp., 142 F. The rule of damages for the difference between the rental payments due and the fair rental value is applied by the Courts by deducting the fair rental value for the remainder of the term from the remaining rent payments due (both sums to be discounted at some proper rate-3% in one case,") and if this sum, as it usually will, exceeds the rents due for one or three years as the case may be, the claim is allowed for the latter amount. It is to be noted, however, that the Act specifically allows damages for breaches of other covenants to be included in the gross claim, although the recovery can only total one year or three years rent.

This might be important if the lease had only a short term to run and there were, for example, covenants to restore or rebuild. 7

It must also be noticed that the rent allowed to be proved may include taxes or other payments which may be held to be in the nature of rent. This is very important both for the purposes of the gross claim and particularly for the purpose of the provable claim for one or three years rent. A number of cases have arisen where the landlord had a deposit for security and the question was raised as to how this should be treated. A leading case 10 holds that the deposit is to be deducted from the provable claim, not from the gross claim, on the ground that a landlord should not obtain an advantage "merely because he has been shrewd or economically powerful enough to have obtained a substantial deposit as security." The Court even suggests that if the deposit exceeds the claim, the surplus should be turned over to the trustee. And if the deposit is held by the landlord for future rents, instead of liquidated damages, a cancellation of the lease by the landlord will require a return of the whole deposit.11 § 311. Use and occupation by trustee. In ordinary bankruptcy the trustee has at least the sixty days granted by the statute to reject or affirm the lease,¹ and even if there is a termination clause which is acted upon, the landlord cannot eject the trustee. In any event he must apply to the Bankruptcy Court as any forcible action even under State Court authority would be in contempt of Court. However, after the period granted to the trustee, or at least in exceptional circumstances after a reasonable time the landlord is entitled to possession. The owner "could not without coming into contempt of court eject the court's officer by force . but he could at once petition the court for possession and the court would be bound to do justice according to the circumstances.' " "It is true that the lessor may be held off for a season by the mere arm of the Court, though, strictly this is an anomaly. 

The period ought to be limited to the most immediate and pressing necessities and the power be exercised with the greatest circumspection." 4

As noted in § 306, supra, there is an important difference between ordinary bankruptcy and Corporate Reorganizations under Chapter X in the length of time that a trustee has to reject a lease. It has been held that the sixty day period does not apply to that Chapter as being inconsistent with the right given the judge to reject leases and therefore the trustee has a reasonable time and in the meantime is liable for use and occupation. It would seem probable that the same holding would be made under 

Chapter XI (Arrangements) Chapter XII (Real Estate Ar rangements) 10 and under Chapter XIII (Wage Earners' Plans),11 as in each of these cases the judge is also given the right to reject contracts with no time limit stated. § 313. Receivership. Because of the comprehensive coverage of the Federal Bankruptcy Act in Chapters X, XI, XII and XIII 

in Reorganizations, Arrangements and Plans, the subject of equity or statutory state receivership is of much less importance than formerly. However, if the Federal Bankruptcy Act is not resorted to, the state court still has jurisdiction to appoint receivers under its general equity powers or under special statutory powers relating to corporations, (a) if the corporation has been dissolved 2 or (b) upon petition of a judgment creditor whose execution has remained unsatisfied for thirty days. Although a trustee in bankruptcy, being vested with the bankrupt's property, may reject or adopt a lease, a receiver in Massachusetts has no such title and cannot affect the obligations of a lease either by rejecting it or becoming an assignee under it.5 

He may, however, take possession of the property for a reasonable time for the purpose of preserving the assets of the debtor and in this event he is liable only for a reasonable rental and not under the covenants of the lease."

Since the receiver cannot affect the obligations of a lease and convert the lessor's rights into a limited provable claim, as can now be done by a trustee in bankruptcy, it would appear that the lessor may enforce, if he can, the lessee's obligation to pay future installments of the rent as they become due, as he could under the old bankruptcy law." and the lessee covenants that, in case of such termination or in case of termination under the provisions of statute by reason of the default of the lessee, the lessee will forthwith pay to the lessor as damages a sum equal to the amount by which the rent and other payments called for hereunder for the remainder of the original term and of any extension thereof exceed the fair rental value of said premises for the remainder of the original term and of any extension thereof, and in addition thereto will furthermore indemnify the lessor during the remainder of the original term and of any extension thereof against all loss and damage suffered by reason of such termination, however caused, first deducting any damages paid as above provided, the loss and damage, if any, for each rent payment period during the remainder of the original term and 367

IX. Waiver,

Notices of any extension thereof to be paid at the end of each such rent payment period.

NOTE: Of course the various bankruptcy laws limit the rights given by this paragraph (see Chapter VIII supra) but they might be of full value under some circumstances and are important in every case. 

No consent or waiver, express or implied, by the lessor, to or of any breach of any covenant, condition or duty of the lessee, shall be construed as a consent or waiver to or of any other breach of the same or any other covenant, condition or duty. Any notice from the lessor to the lessee or from the lessee to the lessor shall be deemed duly served if mailed by registered mail addressed, if to the lessee, at said premises or, if to the lessor, at the place from time to time established for the payment of rent and the customary registered mail receipt shall be conclusive evidence of such service.

II. SHORT FORM LEASE 

Lease, MADE the 1st day of January 1949 A B, lessor, leases to

C. D, lessee, (the expression lessor and lessee including their respective heirs, executors, administrators, successors and assigns) the premises at (Description)

To hold for the term of 2 yrs. from the first day of January 

1949 yielding and paying therefor the rent of twelve hundred (1200) dollars per annum.

And the lessee promises to pay the said rent in equal monthly payments in advance beginning January first 1949 and to quit and deliver up the premises to the lessor, or his attorney, peaceably and quietly, at the end of the term, in as good order and condition, reasonable use and wearing thereof, fire and unavoidable casualties excepted, as the same now are, or may be put into by the said lessor, and to pay the rent as above stated, dur- 368

FORMS 

ing the term, and, for such further time as the lessee may hold the same, and not make or suffer any waste thereof; nor lease, nor underlet, nor permit any other person or persons to occupy or improve the same, or make or suffer to be made any alteration therein, without the approval of the lessor in writing, having been first obtained; and that the lessor shall have the right to view and make improvements, and to enter to expel the lessee, if he shall fail to pay the rent as aforesaid, or make or suffer any strip or waste thereof, or become bankrupt, and such entry shall terminate this lease. 

And provided also, that in case the premises, or any part thereof during the said term, be destroyed or damaged by fire or unavoidable casualty, so that the same shall be thereby rendered unfit for use and habitation, then, and in such case, the rent hereinbefore reserved, or a just and proportional part thereof, according to the nature and extent of the injuries sustained, shall be suspended or abated until the said premises shall have been put in proper condition for use and habitation by the said lessor, or these presents shall thereby be determined and ended at the election of the said lessor. 

In witness whereof, The said parties have hereunto set their hands and seals the day and year first above written.

Assignment to Be Endorsed on Lease. 

Boston, Feb. 4, 1949

In consideration of eight hundred dollars and other good and valuable considerations to be paid by P., of said Boston, the receipt whereof is hereby acknowledged, I do hereby sell, assign, transfer, and set over to the said P., his heirs and assigns, all my right, title, and interest in and to the within written instrument. Witness my hand and seal the day and year above written. 

J. S. (lessee).

Short Form.

Agreement by Assignee to Assume Covenants of Lease. 

In consideration of the foregoing assignment to us made (or, if on separate paper, describe the assignment), we hereby covenant and agree to and with the said F. (lessor) herein named, that we will punctually pay the rent and other charges in said lease to be paid, and that we will keep, fulfill, and perform all the covenants and agreements in said lease to be kept, fulfilled, and performed by the lessee or his assigns. 

In witness whereof, we have hereunto set our hands and seals this fourth day of February, 1949.

PREFACE 

This pamphlet has been prepared under considerable pressure of time, since the Housing and Rent Act of 1949 only became law on April 1st, and Regulations and Orders to May 10th have been included. It is not intended to be a learned treatise on the subject, but is designed to present in readily available form and arrangement, with appropriate comments where necessary, the important current provisions of the law and regulations. Since the Act of 1949 and the regulations under it are only amendments of earlier acts and regulations, they are not officially published in complete form. The authors are concerned here chiefly with lightening the difficulties of the practitioner engaged in this work by helping him to locate the authorities, statutory and regulatory, which, for the most part, are self-explanatory. Judicial authorities are limited to the Supreme Judicial Court of Massachusetts.

The authors acknowledge with thanks the helpful assistance of Professor Richard H. Field, formerly General Counsel for the 

Office of Price Administration, and of James J. Brennan, Esq.,

Chief Rent Attorney of the Eastern Massachusetts Area Rent 

Office, who has made available regulations and information otherwise difficult to obtain. 

Boston, Massachusetts 

May 20, 1949

Faneuil Adams

Federal Rent Control Manual

CHAPTER I HISTORICAL SURVEY § 1. Rent control prior to the 1949 Act. Under the Emergency 

Price Control Act of 1942,¹ rent control was in effect in all but three counties 2 in Massachusetts from the summer of 1942 until July 1, 1947. Maximum rents were administratively established upon the level of rentals in effect on March 1, 1942, subject, however, to adjustments for cause shown. All landlords in the controlled areas were required to register their housing accommodations, specifying the rental in effect and the services given the tenant on the base date.

The 1942 Act was general in its terms and conferred upon the Price Administrator broad powers to establish "generally fair and equitable" rents. The Administrator was also authorized to regulate or prohibit speculative or manipulative renting practices, "including practices relating to recovery of the possession" Pursuant to this power, he imposed by regulation strict control over evictions.

On June 30, 1947, the Emergency Price Control Act of 1942 

was terminated and the Housing and Rent Act of 1947, the provisions of which were to be administered by the Housing Expediter, became effective. The new Act, unlike the old, set forth the specific terms of control and left little to the regulations of the Expediter. It was designed to work a transfer of control from the Federal Government to the states and to local subdivisions of government, as well as to allow for decontrol as circumstances warranted. Since one of the purposes of the 1947 Act was to divide the responsibility for administering the controls among locally selected officials, local advisory boards were appointed by the Housing Expediter upon recommendations from the state governors.

The Act defined housing accommodations as: 

§ 1. 150 U.S.C.A. App. (cited hereafter as Code), secs. 901-946. 

2 Rent control was established in Franklin County effective May 1, 1946, fixing rents at the January 1, 1945 levels. Rents in Dukes and Nantucket counties were not controlled. 

3 Code, sec. 1893. 

3

соз 

Any building, structure, or part thereof, or land appurtenant thereto, or any other real or personal property rented or offered for rent for living or dwelling purposes (including houses, apartments, rooming or boardinghouse accommodations, or other properties used for living or dwelling purposes), together with all privileges, services, furnishings, furniture and facilities connected with the use or occupancy of such property.4 

Controlled housing accommodations included all within this definition except nine expressly exempted classes of premises; namely hotels; motor courts; trailers; tourist homes; new premises completed after February 1, 1947; old premises converted to housing accommodations after February 1, 1947; premises unrented for 24 months between February 1, 1945, and

March 30, 1948, inclusive; premises constructed on or after 

February 1, 1945, and prior to February 1, 1947, and not rented at any time prior to and including June 30, 1947; and certain nonhousekeeping furnished accommodations in single dwelling units.

Further decontrol was allowed on the initiative of the Housing 

Expediter or on the recommendation of local advisory boards.

Decontrol in this manner was final and subsequent recontrol was prohibited.

Rent increases not in excess of 15% were provided where a voluntary written lease was entered into by the landlord and tenant and certain express conditions were complied with. 

Under the Act the maximum rents in effect on June 30, 1947, were continued, and accordingly present maximum rents are in general those originally established under the Emergency Price Control Act of 1942. However, modification of rents were allowed by three methods: (1) adjustment by the Housing Expediter under his independent powers to change maximum rents in the event of hardship (operating loss to landlord) or to correct inequities; (2) adjustment by the Housing Expediter on the recommendation of a local advisory board; and (3) voluntary execution of a lease as referred to above. 

The 1947 Act prohibited eviction of a tenant, otherwise permissible under local law, as long as he continued to pay his rent except for one or more of the following grounds: (1) the violation of an obligation of the tenancy; (2) the commission of a nuisance; (3) the use of the premises for immoral or illegal purposes; (4) the use of the premises for other than dwelling pur- 

4 Code, sec. 1892 (b).

HISTORICAL SURVEY 

§ 1 poses; (5) the recovery of the premises by the landlord for his own or his immediate family's use or the use of a charitable organization; (6) the recovery of the premises for the use of a purchaser of the premises or his immediate family; (7) for the purpose of remodeling or altering the premises in such a way that continuation of the tenancy was impractical; (8) where the landlord sought to withdraw the premises from the housing rental market; or (9) where the premises were acquired by the state for a public improvement. The 1948 amendment imposed a sixty-day written notice upon the landlord if the eviction were based upon the fifth through ninth grounds. 

The only authority retained by the Housing Expediter respecting evictions was the enjoining of illegal evictions under the 

Federal Act. 

The tenant was given the right to recover any overcharge of rent, together with attorney's fees and costs, and if the overcharge were wilful he was entitled to treble damages. Suit had to be commenced within one year."

CHAPTER II SUMMARY OF PRESENT LAW 

§ 2. General. The recent Act, passed March 30, 1949, and effective April 1, 1949, is an amendment of the Housing and Rent

Act of 1947, and, with that Act, represents the present law. 

Leases and adjustments properly made under the earlier Acts are still effective, and the Regulations, under the Act of 1947, except as amended, are still in force. The Act recontrols some housing situations and gives the Housing Expediter broader powers of control over rents and evictions. The Act expires on June 

30, 1950.

CHAPTER III DEFENSE RENTAL AREAS § 5. General-Law. "The term 'defense-rental area' means any part of any area designated under the provisions of the Emergency Price Control Act of 1942, as amended, prior to 

March 1, 1947, as an area where defense activities have resulted or threaten to result in an increase in the rents for housing accommodations inconsistent with the purposes of such Act, in which maximum rents (1) were being regulated under such Act on March 1, 1947, or (2) are established or reestablished pursuant to section 204 (i) (1) or (2) of this title." 1

Comment. All of Massachusetts except Martha's Vineyard and Nantucket constitutes a Defense Rental Area. The references in the above law to sections 204 (i) (1) and (2)2 refer to the power of the Housing Expediter on recommendation of local Advisory Boards to declare new defense rental areas which were never controlled or were controlled and have been decontrolled. 

As there seems to be no practical likelihood that there will be any action along these lines in Massachusetts before the Act expires these sections are not quoted in full. They provide standards for the recommendation of the boards. § 5. 1 Housing and Rent Act of 1947 as amended (cited hereafter as Law), sec. 202(d); Code, sec. 1892(d). 2 Code, sec. 1894 (i) (1) and (2). 8

+ 

CHAPTER IV HOUSING ACCOMMODATIONS § 6. General-Law. "The term 'housing accommodations' 

means any building, structure, or part thereof, or land appurtenant thereto, or any other real or personal property rented or offered for rent for living or dwelling purposes (including houses, apartments, rooming or boarding-house accommodations, and other properties used for living or dwelling purposes) together with all privileges, services, furnishings, furniture, and facilities connected with the use or occupancy of such property." 1 

Regulations. The Regulations merely paraphrase the law. 

Comment. Although the law is very general and by its terms applies to all dwelling facilities there are many exceptions created by law and regulation which are listed in the following section. § 7. Exceptions. Exceptions 1-4 below are excepted from the definition of the term "controlled housing accommodations," and therefore are not subject to the controls applicable thereto. Exceptions 5-10 are called exempted housing rather than decontrolled housing and depend entirely upon regulations made by the Housing Expediter which were in force before the New Act and are still in force. (1) Hotels-Law. "Those housing accommodations, in any establishment which is located in a city of less than 2,500,000 population according to the 1940 decennial census and which is commonly known as a hotel in the community in which it is located, which are occupied by persons who are provided customary hotel services such as maid service, furnishing and laundering of linen, telephone and secretarial or desk service, use and upkeep of furniture and fixtures, and bellboy service." 1 

Regulations. "Accommodations in hotels. (a) In cities of less than 2,500,000 population according to the 1940 decennial census § 6. 1 Law, sec. 202(b); Code, sec. 1892(b). § 7. 1 Law, sec. 202 (c) (1) (A); Code, sec. 1892 (c) (1) (A). 9

$7

those housing accommodations in any hotel which on June 30, 1947, were occupied by persons to whom were provided customary hotel services such as maid service, furnishing and laundering of linen, telephone and secretarial or desk service, use and upkeep of furniture and fixtures, and bellboy services (not necessarily all the types of services named need be provided in all cases as long as enough are provided to constitute customary hotel services usually supplied in establishments commonly known as hotels in the community where they are located). For purposes of this subdivision (a), the term 'hotel' means any establishment which is commonly known as a hotel in the community in which it is located and which provides customary hotel services." 2

Comment. Hotels providing customary hotel services are exempted. The law and regulations also provide for partial recontrol of hotels in cities of over 2,500,000 but as this has no importance in New England these are omitted. (2) Motor Courts, trailers, tourist homes-Law. CHAPTER V  

§ 8. Definition of rent-Law. "The term 'rent' means the consideration, including any bonus, benefit, or gratuity demanded or received for or in connection with the use or occupancy of housing accommodations, or the transfer of a lease of housing accommodations." 1

Regulations. The regulation is identical to the law.² 

Comment. Rent is defined broadly to include consideration of any type received in connection with the use of housing accommodations. The purpose of this definition is to provide against all attempts of evasion by charging for incidental services or by receiving gifts. In this connection the regulations further provide against attempts to evade the law as follows: "(a) General. 

The maximum rents and other requirements provided in this regulation shall not be evaded, either directly or indirectly in connection with the renting or leasing or the transfer of a lease of housing accommodations, by way of absolute or conditional sale, sale with purchase money or other form of mortgage, or sale with option to repurchase or by modification of the practices relating to payment of commissions or other charges or by modification of the services furnished with housing accommodations, or by tying agreement, or otherwise. (b) Purchase of property as condition of renting. Specifically, but without limitation on the foregoing, no person shall require a tenant or prospective tenant to purchase or agree to purchase furniture or any other property as a condition of renting housing accommodations unless the prior written consent of the Expediter is obtained."

(3) General Adjustments-Comment. Under the law the Ex pediter is given power to make general adjustments of rents. 

The section of the law giving him this power is fully quoted in the following section as it applies to individual adjustments also.³ 

In general as well as individual adjustments the Expediter is supposed to consider "fair net operating income" to the landlord. 

In regard to general adjustments there are elaborate provisions of law appointing Advisory Boards which can make recommendations to the Expediter respecting such adjustments. In turn the 

Advisory Boards must hold hearings upon the petition of a representative group of tenants or landlords. The recommendations of the Boards must be substantiated, and applicable law and regulations complied with by the performance of various procedural acts, and an appeal is allowed to the Emergency Court of Appeals from final action. As these provisions are lengthy and not important in individual cases they are printed in Appendix A.

(4) Individual Increases-Comment. Under earlier laws there were set up elaborate standards for individual increases covering several pages of the regulations. These last appeared in section 5 of the Regulations 825. Briefly the grounds included major capital improvements, substantial increase in space, service 20

§ 

or equipment, seasonal adjustment, increase in occupancy, substantial hardship because of increase in operating expenses, inequalities in rent under prevailing rents and others. However, there has been a major change in the new law which requires rents to be maintained "as far as practicable" at levels that will give the landlord a "fair net operating income." The law reads in full, after reciting the establishment of maximum rents quoted in section 10 supra, as follows: 

Law. "Provided, however, That the Housing Expediter shall, by regulation or order, make such individual and general adjustments in such maximum rents in any defense-rental area or any portion thereof, or with respect to any housing accommodations or any class of housing accommodations within any such area or any portion thereof, as may be necessary to remove hardships or to correct other inequities, or further to carry out the purposes and provisions of this title: Provided, however, That the landlord certifies that he is maintaining all services furnished as of the date determining the maximum rent and that he will continue to maintain such services so long as the adjustment in such maximum rent which may be granted continues in effect. In making and recommending individual and general adjustments to remove hardships or to correct other inequities, the Housing Expediter and the local boards shall observe the principle of maintaining maximum rents for controlled housing accommodations, so far as is practicable, at levels which will yield to landlords a fair net operating income from such housing accommodations. In determining whether the maximum rent for controlled housing accommodations yields a fair net operating income from such housing accommodations, due consideration shall be given to the following among other relevant factors: (A) Increases in property taxes; (B) unavoidable increases in operating and maintenance expenses; (C) major capital improvement of the housing accommodations as distinguished from ordinary repair, replacement and maintenance; (D) increases or decreases in living space, services, furniture, furnishings, or equipment; and (E) substantial deterioration of the housing accommodations, other than ordinary wear and tear, or failure to perform ordinary repair, replacement or maintenance." 4

Regulations. The most recent change in the regulations has to do with the details of the allowance of a new ground for in-

"Test year' means the most recent full calendar or fiscal year, or any 12 consecutive months ending not earlier than 90 days before the date the petition is filed." 18

Summarily stated this Regulation allows an increase of the rent so that a landlord of small units (less than five) may net 25% of his gross income, and a landlord of large units (five or more) may net 20%. All ordinary expenses are allowed including depreciation which is limited to the amount in the last Federal Income Tax Return or 21% of the gross income in small units or 16% in large units, whichever is lower. Expenses for amortization and interest are not deductible. The Expediter has issued two documents construing the regulation. The first was a state- 

18 Reg. 825.5(18). 26

§ ment published in the newspapers and the other was a series of questions and answers. 

The first document merely states the substance of the Regulations in narrative form and gives a few examples. It also calls attention to the fact that either the landlord or tenant has a right to appeal under the new procedural regulations (see Chapter VII infra). Ordinarily only one request for relief per year will be considered so that figures for an entire successive year will be available.

The question and answer release goes into various details not immediately apparent from the regulation, for example: a. The rent entered on the petition is the rent legally asked, not the rent actually collected. b. Where there are some rents that cannot be increased (15% leases still in effect) the amount of increase allowed is applied proportionately over all the units, so that the unleased portions do not bear the whole burden of the raise, and the landlord cannot get its full advantage until all the units are free. c. The same apportionment applies where there are commercial units included in the whole property, so that the residential units will not bear the whole increase. d. Insurance deduction is prorated so that, for example, one-third of a threeyear policy is deductible in each year. e. The expense allowable for interior decorating and painting is normally one-third of the total actually spent for the test year and the two preceding years. f. If the costs have gone up during the test year through increase in taxes or otherwise an allowance can be made if a special form is filed, since the object is to have a fair rent at the time the petition is filed. g. Capital expenses must be prorated over the probable life of the improvement, not all taken in the year paid. (5) Individual decreases. § 12. Powers of control and decontrol. 

(1) Areas-Controlled. As stated above in section 5 all Massa chusetts, except Martha's Vineyard and Nantucket, is now controlled, although the Expediter may, upon recommendation of the Advisory Boards, control those areas or recontrol any area that is decontrolled.¹ (2) Areas-Decontrol by Expediter. There appears to be no specific provision like the above covering areas only, but the Expediter has the power to decontrol any rents in an area or portion thereof. The law is as follows: 

"The Housing Expediter is hereby authorized and directed to remove any or all maximum rents before this title ceases to be in effect, in any defense-rental area or portion thereof or with respect to any class of housing accommodations in any such area or portion thereof, if in his judgment the need for continuing maximum rents in such area or portion thereof or with respect to such class of housing accommodations no longer exists, due to sufficient construction of new housing accommodations or when the demand for rental housing accommodations has been otherwise reasonably met. The Housing Expediter is further authorized and directed to remove maximum rents for any or all luxury housing accommodations in any defense-rental area or portion thereof, if in his judgment such action would result in the creation of additional rental units by conversion. The Housing Expediter shall from time to time make surveys with a view to carrying out the purpose of this subsection to decontrol housing accommodations at the earliest practicable time." &

§ § 14. Rights of landlord. 

(1) To security deposit. The landlord may obtain a security. 

deposit of not more than one month's rent in addition to rent paid in advance if such was the custom of the landlord or the area, provided the tenant is allowed not to pay rent for a period commensurate with the deposit.¹ (2) To rely on lease agreement. The landlord may rely on any provisions of the lease or rental agreement not prohibited by the act or regulation.2 

(3) To apply for individual or general increase. The landlord may apply, as above set out (§ 11 (4)), for an upward adjustment of his individual rents. He may also, in combination with other landlords, apply for a general adjustment, or for a removal of maximum rents for any area or part thereof, or any class of housing accommodations.* 3 (4) To evict tenant. The landlord may evict the tenant under certain conditions (see Chapter VI, infra). 

§ 15. Rights and duties of tenant. 

The tenant's duties are to pay the rent allowed and not to violate a substantial obligation of the tenancy. If he does these things he cannot be evicted except for one of the other special grounds referred to in Chapter VI on Eviction. 

Besides being entitled to the benefit of the duties of the landlord as set out in § 13, the tenant may petition for a reduction of his individual rent on one or more of the grounds set out in § 11 (5). He may also, like a landlord, apply with other tenants for general adjustments. He may also have the benefit of the various provisions for enforcement of the Act set out in the following section, including the right to sue for treble damages.

CHAPTER VI EVICTION 

§ 17. General. The 1949 Act reverts to the method of controlling evictions originally adopted by the Emergency Price Control Act of 1942, namely, regulation by the Administrator.¹ 

Under this power the Housing Expediter as such administrator has issued comprehensive regulations, effective as of April 1, 1949, which increase the number of grounds of eviction over those existing under the 1947 Act, but which involve greater strictness as to notice and as to the use of the former grounds. 

These are summarized here and fully printed in Appendix B. 

§ 18. Grounds of eviction. 

(1) Nonpayment of rent. A three-day notice to vacate the premises is required, setting forth, in addition to the material required in all notices (see § 19, infra), a statement of the rent due and the rental periods for which the rent is due. (2) Violation of a substantial obligation of the tenancy. This excludes the obligation to pay rent or to surrender possession. 

Two notices are required, the first, a direction to the tenant to cease the violation, and the second, applicable only if the violation continues, a ten-day notice to vacate the premises. (3) Nuisance or illegal or immoral use. Where the tenant commits or permits a nuisance to continue two notices are again re- • quired, the first a direction to the tenant to cease the nuisance, and the second, applicable only if the nuisance continues, a tenday notice to vacate the premises. Where the tenant uses or permits the use of the premises for immoral or illegal purposes, a ten-day notice to vacate alone is required. (4) Tenant's refusal of access to landlord. If, contrary to the rental agreement, the tenant unreasonably refuses access to the landlord to inspect the premises or to show them to a prospective purchaser, mortgagee, or other person having a legitimate interest, eviction is permissible on a notice of not less than one

§ 19. Notice requirements. In evictions based upon the first seven grounds referred to above (nonpayment of rent, violation of substantial obligation of tenancy, nuisance or illegal or immoral use, refusal of access to landlord, accommodations entirely sublet, public improvement by state, company housing development) the notice required by the Regulations must be given. in writing to the tenant and a copy filed with the Area Rent Office within 24 hours thereafter. The notice must state the ground upon which the landlord relies, the facts necessary to establish the existence of such ground and the date when the tenant is required to surrender possession. Where nonpayment of rent is involved, the notice shall also include the amount of rent due and the rental periods for which it is due. 

No action for obtaining possession of the premises may be commenced by the landlord until the period of the notice (varying from three days to two months as set forth under the discussion of the particular grounds) has expired. At the time of beginning any action based on one or more of such seven grounds, the landlord must give written notice to the Area Rent Office, stating the title of the case, its number if possible, the court where filed, the name and address of the tenant and the ground of removal. § 20. Eviction certificates. In evictions based upon the eighth through twelfth grounds referred to above (occupancy by owner, occupancy by contract-purchaser, alterations or demolishing, landlord as tax-exempt organization, withdrawal from rental market), no tenant shall be evicted unless on the petition of the landlord the Housing Expediter certifies that the landlord may pursue his local remedies after the expiration of the appropriate waiting period (varying from three to six months as set forth under the discussion of the particular grounds) from the date of the filing of the petition or from the date of the issuance of the certificate in the one case of the additional two-month waiting period of the contract-purchaser who does not have the right to immediate possession under his contract.

The Expediter may waive all or part of any waiting period if extreme hardship would result to the landlord by reason of exceptional circumstances. § 21. Local law. Nothing in the Regulations authorizes the removal of a tenant unless such removal is allowed by the local 41

§  

law. Furthermore no provision of the Regulations will be construed to prohibit a landlord who has obtained a certificate from the Expediter from serving such notice as may be required by local law prior to the expiration of the specified waiting period, provided possession is not demanded until after such expiration. § 22. Miscellaneous. The Regulations do not apply to certain cases of subtenants and of public housing developments, nor to cases in which judgment has been entered prior to April 1, 1949. 

In cases where the landlord has given notice prior to April 1, 1949, under the 1947 Act, or where no notice was required and court proceedings were pending on April 1, 1949, the landlord need not comply with the notice requirements of the new Regulations; and if the ground is one for which the new Regulations require a certificate of the Housing Expediter, the waiting period may be reduced, taking into consideration the time elapsed since the original notice was given by the landlord. 42

CHAPTER VII PROCEDURE § 23. General. The question of how either landlord or tenant can obtain relief has been much simplified by the adoption of "Rent Procedural Regulation 2," which went into effect April 14, 1949. Before this there was a Regulation in effect known as "Rent Procedural Regulation 1," which outlined the procedure much more briefly and set forth the procedure, particularly on behalf of the tenant, with much less clarity. This Regulation is no longer in effect, except for proceedings begun before April 14, 1949, and then only until an order is entered by the Area Rent Director. After that the new Regulation takes effect, so for all practical purposes the new one is the only one of importance.

The Regulation sets up the procedure to be followed by either the landlord or tenant in obtaining relief from Regulations or orders. There are three steps. 

(1) Action before Area Rent Director. This provides for the filing of a simple petition either by the landlord or tenant on forms prescribed; the Area Rent Director is also empowered to initiate proceedings. In any event, notice is given to all parties and an oral hearing can be had if the Director so desires. There are provisions for allowing the eliciting of evidence by interrogatories or otherwise. (2) Review by Regional Housing Expediter. In the event that the landlord or tenant is dissatisfied with the decision of the Area 

Rent Director, he may ask for a review by the Regional Housing

Expediter. This is really a de novo hearing, and the Regional 

Expediter has the same powers as the Area Rent Director in allowing hearings, eliciting evidence, etc. As in the prior hearing due notice must be given to all parties including a chance for response and rebuttal. 

(3) Appeals to Housing Expediter. These are appeals in the strict sense, and ordinarily do not allow for introduction of new 

§ 23. 1 The Regulation is summarized in Appendix B. 

43

§  

evidence or oral hearings, although in the discretion of the Expediter and under certain circumstances the issues can be broadened and hearings held. There are rules for procedure including proper form of papers, briefs, etc., and again ample chance is given to all parties to meet any issue that may be raised. These appeals lie from the decision of the Regional Housing Expediter, or direct from the Area Rent Director if the order of the Director has been entered on remand from the Regional Housing Expediter.

The Regulation is very long but the provisions which will normally be needed are summarized in Appendix D, so that anyone wishing to take any steps will know the general requirements and order of procedure. In any event forms must be obtained from the Area Rent Office.

APPENDIX B REGULATION 825.6 

Eviction Regulations "§ 825.6 Removal of tenant—(a) Restrictions on removal of tenant.

So long as the tenant continues to pay the rent to which the landlord is entitled, no tenant shall be removed from any housing accommodations by action to evict or to recover possession, by exclusion from possession, or otherwise, nor shall any person attempt such removal or exclusion from possession, notwithstanding that such tenant has no lease or that his lease or other rental agreement has expired or otherwise terminated, and regardless of any contract, lease, agreement or obligation heretofore or hereafter entered into which provides for surrender of possession, or for entry of judgment upon the tenant's confession for breach of the covenants thereof, or which otherwise provides contrary hereto, except on one or more of the grounds specified in this paragraph (a), or unless the landlord has obtained a certificate in accordance with paragraph (c) of this section: Provided, however, That no provisions of this section shall be construed to authorize the removal of a tenant unless such removal is authorized under local law. (1) Violating substantial obligation of tenancy. The tenant is violating a substantial obligation of his tenancy, other than an obligation to pay rent or an obligation to surrender possession of the housing accommodations, and has continued or failed to cure such violation after a written notice by the landlord that the violation cease. (2) Nuisance or illegal or immoral use. Under the local law, the tenant (i) is committing or permitting a nuisance in the housing accommodations and such nuisance continues after written notice to the tenant that the same shall cease or (ii) is using or permitting a use of such housing accommodations for an immoral or illegal purpose. (3) Tenant's refusal of access to landlord. The tenant has unreasonably refused the landlord access to the housing accommodations for the purpose of inspection or of showing the accommodations to a prospective purchaser, mortgagee, or prospective mortgagee, or other person having a legitimate interest therein: Provided, however, That such refusal shall not be ground for removal or eviction if such inspection or showing of the accommodations is contrary to the provisions of the tenant's lease or other rental agreement. (4) Accommodations entirely sublet. The tenant's lease or other rental agreement has expired or otherwise terminated, and at the time of termination the occupants of the housing accommodations are subtenants or other persons who occupied under a rental agreement with the tenant, and no part of the accommodations is used by the tenant as his dwelling. 50 [Hall Supp]

APPENDIX B 

1 (5) Landlord is a state or political subdivision thereof. The housing accommodations have been acquired by a state or political subdivision thereof for the purpose of making a public improvement and are rented temporarily pending the construction of such improvement. (6) Company housing. The housing accommodations are part of a company housing development in which occupancy has customarily been limited to employees of the landlord, and the tenant is no longer his employee. (b) Notice required. (1) No tenant shall be removed or evicted from housing accommodations by court process or otherwise and no action or proceeding shall be commenced for such purpose upon any of the grounds permitted in paragraph (a) of this section unless and until the landlord shall have given written notice to the Area Rent Office and to the tenant as provided in this paragraph (b) (1). 

Every such notice to a tenant to vacate or surrender possession of housing accommodations shall state the ground under this section upon which the landlord relies for removal or eviction of the tenant, the facts necessary to establish the existence of such ground, and the date when the tenant is required to surrender possession. Where the ground for removal or eviction of a tenant is nonpayment of rent such notice shall include a statement of the rent due and the rental period or periods for which such rent is due. A written copy of every notice required by this paragraph (b) (1) shall be filed with the Area Rent Office within 24 hours after such notice is given to the tenant.

Every such notice shall be given to the tenant at least the following period of time prior to the date specified therein for the surrender of possession and to the commencement of any action for removal or eviction: (a) Where the ground specified in the notice for such removal or eviction is nonpayment of rent, not less than three days. (b) Where the notice specifies one or more of the grounds stated in paragraphs (a) (1) and (a) (2) of this section for such removal or eviction, not less than ten days. (c) Where the notice specifies the ground stated in paragraph (a) (3) of this section for such removal or eviction, not less than one month. (d) Where the notice specifies one or more of the grounds stated in paragraphs (a) (4), (a) (5) and (a) (6) of this section for such removal or eviction, not less than two months.

If judgment for possession is sought by virtue of a confession of judgment or by virtue of a warrant of attorney authorizing confession of such judgment against the tenant, the date of commencement of the action as referred to in this section shall be deemed to be the date of the filing in court of the first papers in the proceedings for the entry of such judgment. (2) At the time of commencing any action to remove or evict a tenant, on any ground stated in paragraph (a) of this section the landlord shall give written notice thereof to the Area Rent Office, 51

stating the title of the case, the number of the case where that is possible, the court in which it is filed, the name and address of the tenant, and the ground under said paragraph on which removal or eviction is sought. (c) Eviction certificate; grounds for issuance. No tenant shall be removed or evicted on grounds other than those stated in paragraph (a) of this section, unless on petition of the landlord the Housing Expediter certifies that the landlord may pursue his remedies in accordance with the requirements of local law. The certificate shall authorize the pursuit of local remedies at the expiration of the waiting period specified in paragraph (d) of this section. The Expediter shall so certify if he finds that removals or evictions of the character proposed are not inconsistent with the purposes of the act or this regulation and would not be likely to result in the circumvention or evasion thereof. The Expediter shall so find in the following cases: (1) Occupancy by owner. Where the landlord, who is the owner of the housing accommodations, establishes that he seeks in good faith to recover possession thereof for his immediate and personal use and occupancy as housing accommodations, or for the immediate and personal use and occupancy as housing accommodations by a member or members of his immediate family (see definition of "immediate family" at the end of this subparagraph (1)): Provided, however, That: (a) Where the housing accommodations are located in a structure or premises which contain more than two housing accommodations and the housing accommodations or structure or premises are owned by two or more persons not constituting a cooperative corporation or association (husband and wife as owners being considered 'one owner for this purpose), no certificate shall be issued under this paragraph (c) (1) for occupancy of more than one housing accommodation and then only if none of the co-owners is already in occupancy of any housing accommodation in such structure or premises; 

(b) In the case of housing accommodations in a structure or premises owned by a cooperative corporation or association, no certificate shall be issued by the Expediter to a purchaser of stock or other evidence of interest in such cooperative, who is entitled by reason of such ownership of stock or other evidence of interest to possession of such housing accommodations by virtue of a proprietary lease or otherwise, unless stock or other evidence of interest in the cooperative has been purchased by persons who are tenants in occupancy of at least 65 per cent of the housing accommodations in the structure or premises and are entitled by reason of such ownership to proprietary leases of housing accommodations in the structure or premises; (c) Where the owner or owners purchased and thereby acquired title to the housing accommodations on or after April 1, 1949, no certificate shall be issued under this paragraph (c) (1) unless such owner or owners made a payment or payments of principal totaling at least 10 per cent of the purchase price, but this requirement shall not apply where the purchaser is a veteran of World War II, who, by virtue of his status as such, obtained a loan for use in purchasing such 52

housing accommodations which was guaranteed in whole or in part by the Administrator of Veterans Affairs. 

For purposes of this paragraph (c) (1), the term "immediate family" includes only a son, son-in-law, daughter, daughter-in-law, father, father-in-law, mother, mother-in-law, stepchild and adopted child. (2) Occupancy by contract-purchaser. Where it is established that a person has an enforceable contract to purchase the housing accommodations, and that he seeks in good faith to recover possession thereof for his immediate and personal use and occupancy as housing accommodations, or for the immediate and personal use and occupancy as housing accommodations by a member or members of his immediate family (as defined in subparagraph (1) of this paragraph); Provided, however, that: (a) Where such purchase contract does not give the contract purchaser the right of immediate possession to the housing accommodations, no certificate shall be issued until after title has been transferred to the contract purchaser; and (b) It is established that such contract purchaser, if title were transferred, would be entitled to a certificate under subparagraph (1) of this paragraph. (3) Alterations or remodeling. Where a landlord establishes that he seeks in good faith to recover possession for the immediate purpose of substantially altering or remodeling the housing accommodations, for continued use as housing accommodations, in a manner which cannot practicably be done with the tenant in possession, or for the immediate purpose of demolishing them, provided that the landlord has obtained such approval for the proposed alterations or remodeling or demolition as may be required by federal, state and local law. (4) Landlord is tax-exempt organization. Where the landlord establishes that it is an organization exempt from taxation under section 101 (6) of the Internal Revenue Code, and that it seeks in good faith to recover possession of the housing accommodations for the immediate and personal use and occupancy as housing accommodations by members of its staff. (5) Withdrawal from rental market. 

Where the landlord establishes that he seeks in good faith to recover possession of the housing accommodations for the immediate purpose of (a) making a permanent conversion to commercial use by substantially altering or remodeling them or (b) personally making a permanent use of them for nonhousing purposes or (c) permanently withdrawing them from both the housing and nonhousing rental markets without any intent to sell the housing accommodations. ing period shall extend at least until two months from the date the certificate is issued; (3) In any case where the Expediter finds that by reason of exceptional circumstances extreme hardship would result to the landlord, he may waive all or part of the waiting period. (e) Change of intention. Any certificate issued under paragraph (c) of this section shall not be used in connection with any action to remove or evict a tenant unless such removal or eviction is sought for the purpose specified in the certificate.

In the event that the landlord's intentions or circumstances so change that the premises, possession of which is sought, will not be used for the purpose specified in the certificate, the certificate shall thereupon be null and void. The landlord shall immediately notify the Area Rent Director in writing and surrender the certificate for cancellation. (f) Local law. No provision of this section shall be construed to prohibit a landlord who has obtained a certificate under paragraph (c) of this section from serving, prior to the expiration of the waiting period specified in said certificate, such notice or notices as may be required by the local law, provided that such notice or notices do not demand surrender of possession until after expiration of said waiting period. (g) Exceptions. The provisions of this section do not apply to: (1) Subtenants. A subtenant or other person who occupies or occupied under a rental agreement with the tenant, where removal or eviction of the subtenant or other such occupant is sought by the landlord of the tenant, unless the rental agreement between the landlord and tenant contemplated the subletting by the tenant of the entire accommodations or substantially all of the individual units therein, or unless under the local law there is a tenancy relationship between the landlord and the subtenant or other such occupant. (2) Public housing. Notwithstanding any other provisions of this section, the United States or any State or local public agency may maintain an action or proceeding to recover possession of any housing accommodations operated by it where such action or proceeding is authorized by the statute or regulations under which such accommodations are administered. APPENDIX C 

REGULATIONS 825.81 (a), (b) AND (e), 825.82-825.87

Rooming-House Regulations-Summary 

825.81 Definitions-substantially the same as in Housing Regulations, except that there are added definitions of "Other Establishments" and of "Rooms" to which this regulation applies: 'Rooms' means a room or group of rooms, not constituting an apartment, rented or offered for rent as a housing accommodations unit in a rooming house, hotel or other establishment. The erm inc es ground rented as trailer space"; "Other Establishments' means multiple unit establishments, other than hotels or rooming houses, containing more than two rooms (see definition of room) rented or offered for rent on a short time basis of daily, weekly or monthly occupancy." "C 825.81 (a) Regulation applies to all rooms in rooming houses, other establishments and such hotel rooms as are not decontrolled (not important in New England) and to accommodations voluntarily brought under this regulation under 825.81 (e) infra. 

825.81 (b) Specifies certain decontrolled and exempted housing as follows: Farming tenants, service employees, rooms of charitable or religious organizations used to carry out purposes of the organization, entire structures containing rooms, rooms in non-profit clubs certified by Expediter and rooms in college fraternity or sorority houses so certified, resort housing (see Text, § 7(10)); rooms in hotels in cities of less than 2,500,000, motor courts, transient trailer space, tourist homes, rooms in other establishments giving hotel service, nonhousekeeping furnished accommodations of two or less tenants in the landlord's house and new and additional housing as referred to in Text, § 7(3). 

825.81 (e) The landlord of a building with one or more furnished rooms may elect to bring his building under this regulation rather than the Housing Regulation with the consent of the Expediter, and may revoke the same also with the Expediter's consent. 

825.82 Contains a general prohibition against charging more than maximum rents and states that reducing services is accepting higher rent, and provides that tenant cannot be required to change his term of occupancy.

Where, at the maximum rent date, the room was rented on a weekly or monthly basis the landlord shall continue to offer the room on that basis, except that he is not required to rent for that term more than the greatest number of rooms rented for that term at the maximum rent date, but if the landlord had a seasonal practice of renting 56

APPENDIX C 

rooms for different lengths of time, he may request approval of this from the Administrator.

A tenant on a daily or weekly basis may request a change to a weekly or monthly basis unless landlord is renting for such term a number of rooms equal to the number he is required to rent for that term as above.

The Expediter is given broad authority to determine questions under the above paragraph and to require the renting on a weekly or monthly basis in appropriate cases. 

There are long and elaborate provisions for deposits; generally speaking they forbid deposits of more than one month's rent, and even then they are allowed only if it was the practice and if the tenant can stay on until his deposit is exhausted. 

825.83 Landlord must maintain services, etc. that were originally given plus or minus legal adjustments, if any. 

825.84 Maximum Rents. These are substantially the same as in the Housing Regulations (see Text, § 10). There are special provisions concerning meals with rooms. Here an apportionment has to be made in the general charge for both. The landlord cannot insist on meals as a condition of letting rooms unless that was the practice on the maximum rent date. 

825.85 Adjustments (both up and down, and including allowance for seasonal adjustments) are made on the same general bases as under the Housing Regulations, which are fully covered in the text. 

825.86 Evictions. These are limited (besides non-payment of rent) to (1) violations of substantial obligation of tenancy; (2) nuisance or illegal or immoral use; (3) unreasonable refusal of access to landlord; and (4) company housing. Notice must be given in the manner provided by the Housing Eviction Regulations, except that the period for all notices under these regulations is ten days instead of the varying periods there provided. 

Eviction certificates must be obtained which shall require a delay of three months, unless the Expediter finds it causes exceptional hardship to the landlord.

There is a general provision that the Expediter may grant such a certificate "if he finds that the removals or evictions of the character proposed are not inconsistent with the purposes of this Act" but there are no directions to him to grant such certificates, as in the Housing Regulations, for occupancy by the owner or contract purchaser, alterations and remodeling or withdrawal from rental market. 

However, sub-tenants or daily tenants who have not been in more than thirty days are not protected. 

825.87 Provides for registration and keeping of records; notice of change of landlord and the posting by the landlord in each room rented the maximum rent and whether meals are required. 57

REGULATIONS 840.101-123, 840.125-134, 840.136-138, 840.141-142

Rent Procedural Regulation 2-Summary 

Note. This Regulation applies to all proceedings begun on or after 

April 14, 1949, and to reviews and appeals of orders entered after 

April 1949 on petitions filed before that date.

I. Action before the Area Rent Director 

840.101 This provides generally that administrative proceedings before the Area Rent Director shall be had either on a petition of a landlord or a tenant or on his own initiative and in any event both parties shall have notice and opportunity to be heard. 

840.102-107 Any landlord or tenant may file a petition for adjustment or relief. A landlord must also file a statement on a prescribed form that he is maintaining services. 

Petitions shall be filed on prescribed forms, one original and one copy, and the copy shall be given by the director to the other party. 

The other party has seven days to file a written response, also original and copy, the copy being sent to the petitioner. Seven days more are allowed for a rebuttal by the petitioner, served in a similar manner.

Both response and rebuttal must be limited to the issues raised in the original petition. 

Joint petitions may be filed if there are common grounds and the director may make investigations and require reports. 

840.108 If the Area Director acts on his own initiative he shall serve notices on both the landlord and tenant who shall have seven days to make a response. 

840.109, 840.111 The Director has broad powers over the proceeding. He may dismiss it if it fails to comply with the formalities; mark it for an oral hearing if he desires, or, in his discretion, at the request of a party (840.111); provide for the introduction of evidence if he gives notice and allows response; require the parties to appear and, of course, grant or deny the petition in whole or in part.

An order entered by the Director shall be effective and final subject to review or appeal, or may be revoked or modified provided due notice of intention to revoke or modify is served on the parties and no review is pending.

An order entered after remand from the Housing Expediter shall be subject to appeal to him again. 

840.110 Landlord may file a statement in affidavit form with 

Director to elicit information by interrogatories or otherwise or to obtain documentary evidence of facts or documents subject to the 58

APPENDIX D 

control of the director which are not subject to the control of the landlord.

II. Review by Regional Housing Expediter 

This is a de novo review, not an appeal in the strict sense. 

840.112 An original and one copy of an application for review and all accompanying evidence and objections shall be filed on prescribed forms, except that evidence submitted before the Area Rent Director shall not be re-submitted. These shall be filed fifteen days after the date of the order to be reviewed, and will ordinarily be dismissed if not so filed, and copies shall be served on the other party.

Joint applications on common grounds may be filed and the Expediter may require the filing of separate applications or consolidated applications. 840.113 

Orders compelling refunds may be stayed if the landlord has made proper application and filed cash or certified checks that may be used if he eventually loses. 

840.114-115 Responses to applications (original and copy) may be filed in ten days from the application and shall be served on the other party, and the applicant is then given ten days further for rebuttal in a similar manner (840.115). 

840.116 The Regional Expediter has the same powers over hearings before him as does the Area Director in his hearings (see 840.109, supra), plus the power to affirm, revoke or modify in whole or part the order of the Area Director and to terminate or reinstate an eviction certificate.

His orders are effective and may be modified similarly to those of the Area Director (840.108). 

840.117 Where a tenant files an application for review of an eviction certificate within fifteen days the certificate shall be stayed until twenty days after the review order, provided that any waiting period in the certificate shall not be affected by this (unless such waiting period expires before the stay), and further provided that if the review is frivolous, dilatory or not made in good faith the stay may be terminated. 

840.118-119 Provisions re evidence not subject to landlord's control and oral hearing are similar to those in hearings before the Area Director.

III. Appeals to Housing Expediter 

In these appeals no new evidence may ordinarily be introduced by the parties.

The Expediter may introduce or allow evidence in his discretion. 

840.120 Any landlord affected by a maximum rent regulation or any landlord or tenant affected by an order may appeal from any decision of the Regional Housing Administrator or directly from the decision of an Area Rent Director issued after remand. 

840.121 The scope of the appeal is limited to briefs and arguments on the record and no new evidence shall be introduced unless 59

it is newly discovered or was impossible to advance and is allowed on motion. 

840.122 The appeal shall be filed within twenty days of the order unless there are special circumstances to justify the delay. The appeal shall be filed with the Certifying Officer, Office of the Housing Expediter, Washington 25, D. C., except that an appeal against a regulation shall be filed with the Area Rent Director who shall transmit it to the Housing Expediter with additional material. Copies of appeals, documents, briefs, etc., shall be filed with the appellee. 

Copies and papers shall be typed. 

840.123 The appeal shall contain names and addresses of all appealing parties and where they may receive communications; an identification of the regulation or order appealed from; a clear, concise and separately numbered statement of the objections; a similar statement of the facts and of the relief or specific changes asked for and an oath or affirmation, which shall include those facts alleged on information and belief, plus a statement that copies have been filed with the appellee. 

840.125 Joint appeals may be filed only where at least one ground is common and these appeals may be treated as several or consolidated. 

840.126 Stays orders compelling refunds pending appeals, if proper procedure has been taken under 840.113 (supra). 

840.127 Stays eviction certificates pending appeals as in 840.117 (supra). 

840.128 Provides for responses to appeals after service of notice on the other party within 15 days. The response shall be limited to the proceedings and no new evidence may be introduced without a special request and a showing that the evidence is newly discovered or impossible to present at prior hearings. 

840.129 Briefs (original and 3 copies) are to be filed with the appeal or response unless special leave is obtained. 

840.130 The Expediter may himself put in new evidence or direct any party to do so, and a chance must be given for rebuttal. 

840.131 Oral evidence is received only on special leave and a hearing given on 5 days' notice. A request for evidence not under landlord's control may be made only if such evidence is necessary for a determination of the case. On an appeal from the Regional 

Housing Expediter this privilege is further limited to cases where the Expediter has introduced evidence, where such request was made and denied in prior hearings, or where it could not reasonably have been made before. 

840.132 Any person may submit evidence in support of a regulation by affidavit and such statements may be used in pending or future appeals upon due notice to the appellant. 

840.133-134 The Expediter may take action on appeals similar to that of the Regional Housing Expediter (840.116), and shall give reasons for any opinion or order (840.134). 

840.136-138 Any person may ask for an official interpretation of a regulation or order, in an actual case only. Such interpretations 60

APPENDIX D 

shall be written and signed by the Housing Expediter, the General 

Counsel or Assistant General Counsel in interpretations of general applicability, and by these or any regional attorney or chief rent attorney in the case of particular interpretations. Unless of general applicability they shall apply only to the particular case and shall only be regarded as official if issued as herein provided. 

840.141 The effective dates of filing for notices and statements are when received, or the date of postmark if properly addressed and later received, with a further provision that if a date occurs on a Saturday, Sunday or legal holiday the next business day is sufficient for actual filing. 

840.142 Governs service of papers which shall be mailed, telegraphed, served personally or left at the residence or place of business. Verified personal returns, registered mail slips or telegraph receipts are evidence of service, and if served by unregistered mail an affidavit is required. 61
